newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Swiss negotiators set EU a transport policy poser.
newsitem.headline: Swiss negotiators set EU a transport policy poser.

text.p: The fate of heavy lorries on European Union roads will be at the heart of discussions on Thursday when EU transport ministers debate Swiss proposals to open their Alpine routes to 40-tonne lorries.

Ministers are due to hear a European Commission report on talks with Switzerland and agree tactics for the next stage of negotiations with Berne, an Irish diplomat told reporters ahead of the meeting in Luxembourg.
Discussions will involve a broad political debate on the EU's lorry pricing policy, said the diplomat, whose country holds the EU's six-month presidency.
The talks themselves, part of a package of bilateral issues under discussion since early 1995, aim to allow EU lorries greater access to, and transit through, Switzerland.
The EU has sought immediate access for its trucks to Switzerland's main industrial centres, while Berne wants an access deal to include the right for reciprocal competition in road haulage services.

Linked to access and transit questions is Switzerland's proposal for a phased abolition of its current 28-tonne limit on all lorries, allowing 34-tonne vehicles onto Swiss roads from the start of 2001 and 40 tonners from 2005.

In return Switzerland plans to introduce scaled charges for all lorries on its roads reflecting their infrastructure damage and "nuisance cost" -- a figure based on the amount of noise and pollution caused by the vehicle and associated health effects.
A Commission official said Austria and France objected to the plan because they fear traffic will be diverted onto their roads, while other nations oppose the increased costs.
Countries also worry that the plan could set a precedent for the EU's own policy, a fear fuelled by the Commission's recent enthusiasm for the idea.

Negotiators on both sides are also mindful of the need to satisfy the group holding the ultimate say -- Swiss voters whose 1992 "no" vote to closer ties with the bloc led to the current state of affairs.
"There is no alternative to the current proposal since it is the basis for long-term regulation of issues which are at the heart of the concerns of Swiss people," said a Swiss diplomat.

Bilateral talks on questions such as the elimination of non-tariff trade barriers, air transport liberalisation, scientific research and the free movement of labour have run in parallel to those on road transport.
Conclusion of the package, possibly by early 1997, may yet turn on what happens with heavy lorries.
